utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. The Chamber still owes you a decision on an objection made yesterday since the existence of wounded patients and hospital cannot be said to have no relevance at all. The Defence is allowed to question the witness on -- so to continue its line of questioning. This does not mean that similar questions on the same subject would be allowed for each witness. That means for this witness at this moment, you may continue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Madam Usher, could you please bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the meantime, I believe that I will need about five minutes at the end of this session to address certain matters, perhaps some problems maybe. Just three minutes or five minutes to include the response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Lazic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You still hear me in a language you understand, I take it, since you are wishing us good morning as well. Dr. Lazic, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For interpretation purposes, I am going to ask you to slow down when you answer, please. Thank you. Yesterday we broke off at the time when we were talking about war injuries. And the question that I would like to ask you a the following: How could you explain that children were victims of war injuries, that is, of artillery weapons, as you said it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was in the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the Serb forces, and in that area, as I said already, there are about 100.000 people living there in five Sarajevo municipalities. And I can say that throughout the war, all primary schools, secondary schools, they all worked except when there were fierce clashes, and the schools were not working then, which means that families and children lived in that area. The children were going to school, moving about, coming back from school. And because this is a relatively long period of time, children went out, they didn't stay at home. They knew about areas where they were supposed to go and areas where they were not supposed to go. But when there were sudden artillery shelling or infantry firing from the buildings or facilities that were on the other side of the demarcation line, casualties were caused. Because, as I said, children were often outside. I have to explain, there were a lot of wounded children. And because this is a city, urban space, I am saying that the shells were falling on the asphalt. So ricochets were very strong, very intense. And a lot of the shrapnels caused injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, every time I am looking at your testimony, I am re-reading it, which is why I am not looking at you. You say that suddenly shells could fall. What were the targets that were targeted by these shells in the city, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How could he know that? He is asking all that line of questioning questions just inviting the witness to speculate well outside of his competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that this is not outside of a competence of someone who may have seen shells falling, that he may have seen what they were falling on. Perhaps it is out of the competence of some people, but not of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in the Defence case, I think it has been often argued that sometimes shells fall where they might not have been intended to fall. Why don't you ask the facts, that is, where the shells fell. And then we could come to the next question as to whether the witness has any knowledge on whether where the shell fell was where the shell was intended to fall. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase or phrase my question in such a way. That is what I wanted to say. So I am going to ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you have a knowledge on the location where shells were falling, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in Ilidza for the first two or three months, I lived in the very centre of Ilidza, and because the work at the hospital there was a lot of work and I was by myself. They had to take me about 20 times to the hospital and back, and the road was very dangerous. So after two, three, months, I moved. And until the end of my stay in Sarajevo, I lived at the hospital. I went out of the hospital for the first few months so I would travel to and from hospital, and I moved about regularly on a daily basis. So I can say that on several occasions, I was able to see when the shells were falling. And on several occasions was very dangerous for myself included. I could say that knowing this terrain, the shells, from what I could see as they were falling, they were falling on the urban spaces. But it is a very densely populated part, mixing army and civilian population. So one could explain that almost always nearby there was a military facility. So what I am saying is that civilian and military were very near each other. The military facilities were very nearby. So it wasn't possible to distinguish civilian facilities from military facilities, and some civilian facilities were used as military facilities. So perhaps it wasn't deliberately targeted, but there were civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In other words, what you are saying is that in this Sarajevo that you are describing, there was a kind of mix between purely civilian and purely military facilities. Is this how I am meant to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, if I understood your answer correctly, you said there could have been some firing errors linked to these problems. In the Sarajevo that you knew, in the period of the war, were there many targets that you yourself were able to identify as being obviously military targets or of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly many facilities in this parts of town since it was a military unit, and it had its commands in certain parts of the city. And commands were located in buildings. It had its quartermasters, kitchens, and light and heavy weapons were located, and there were soldiers -- soldiers were not stationed there. They would go to the front line and return home. But there were a large number of officers and uncommissioned officer whose were working there, and they were stationed in civilian facilities in that part of Sarajevo where I was. Practically before the war, there were no military facilities except for some barracks they were outside of the urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, since you have known these facts during the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. war, what do you know about the situation, about the other situation from the other side of the line in Sarajevo about these matters that interest us, that is, the mix and the number of civilian and military target?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this from several sources. First of all, from the medical personnel and the people who, during the war, would leave the city under the control of the Muslim forces and would cross over to the parts of the town that was under control of Serb forces. Also on TV, because you were able, in the city, to watch both the Serb TV and the Bosnia-Herzegovina TV and the Croatian TV, I was able to watch on a daily basis what was happening in that part of town. And also, with the naked eye, I was able to see the parts of town that were under the control of the Muslim forces. So the demarcation line was so small, sometimes a street, sometimes half a street, somewhere it was one house. And then there were some buildings where six or seven doors were Serb, under the control of Serb forces the other immediate Muslim forces. It was a very narrow space. So with the naked eye, you were able to see. So officially, just ten days after I arrived going along a street in Ilidza, I literally went into the part of town which was not under the Serb control it was the Butmir locality. So this is a very narrow space, and it is possible to know what is happening on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Doctor. Now, to summarise, what was the situation on the other side of the line like, on this point that we spoke about? Was it comparable? Was it completely different, in a nutshell, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I knew, I would say it was very similar, if not completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doctor, I would like us now to focus on the question of combat. Were there clashes, was there combat? I believe this is obvious, but could you tell us on which -- how frequent was it? Was it on a daily basis? Was it less frequent, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo is one of the theatres of war of the part of former Bosnia-Herzegovina where there were daily combat. There would be some ceasefire, some truces for several days. They were mostly not respected, but combat was on a daily basis. There was clashes from the town and also outside towards our part of town. So there were daily clashes with the use of practically any kind of conventional weapons with the exception of Air Force, so any infantry artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was the intensity and the frequency of the shellings that was coming from the other side of the line, that is, from the Muslim lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, we are -- we don't know exactly where we are talking about. And it goes back to the original objection about the relevance of all of this. But now we are taking it a step further. The doctor has said that he lived at the hospital, at Zica hospital. We don't know where that is. He said that his hospital from Vogosca going right around to Rajlovac, et cetera. Where are we talking about? Which lines are we talking about? The ones towards Nedzarici, which would be about seven miles where the Zica would be which is the subject of the indictment, or the one somewhere else towards Croatia? If we are asking about where these combats and these lines took place, the counsel should specify in respect of which lines, which areas. The doctor has already testified that his hospital covered a huge area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness said that he lived in the hospital; that is true. He also said that he had the occasion to visit all of these neighbourhoods, and also even neighbourhoods outside of the line. Furthermore, I believe that someone is perfectly well placed considering the frequency of people who were coming, the patients, of the war injuries. So if -- did he stay four days without doing anything or was that never the case? I believe this is a perfect witness to find out whether injuries from shellings happened on a daily basis or not. Whether it was in Ilidza or Grbavica or elsewhere, I am sure that the witness will tell us, if he knows. And I don't think that this should be objected to or could be objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are talking about witnesses mainly a fact of cause. If the witness has observed anything at the front lines, then he could tell us at what front lines he saw what, how often he was there. If he was in the hospital, and you say it might have been that for a couple of days no patients came in, I think that is a fair question to the witness. But whether there was shelling or not based upon his observations on how many patients came in, that is one step further, that is, to ask the witness to draw conclusions. So if you say were there ever a couple of days where came in no patient with shrapnel wounds, for example, that is fair. I think there is no question about the witness could testify about that. But let's try to make a clear distinction between facts and inferences to be drawn from those facts. If you would please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, could you tell us, according to you professional personal experience, could you tell us about the frequency at which civilian or military injuries, how frequently were patients brought to you who were injured by shrapnels?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on average there were seven injured people a day, which doesn't mean that there were seven injured people per day. But sometimes it was fewer, sometimes it was more. There were very rare days that there were no injured because this is a very large space we are talking about. And the percentage, I can tell you, the percentage of artillery injuries compared to the percentage of injuries which were caused by infantry weapons, with the wounds sclopetarium of the infantry weapons, there were about 40 per cent of artillery-caused injuries, and about 60 per cent there were injuries that were caused by infantry weapons. I can say that the hospital was located on a -- very close to the demarcation line, towards Mount Igman, there was 1500 meters as the crow flies. And in the direction of the parts of the town held by the Muslim forces, about 2,000 meters, which means from the window of the hospital I was able to see very clearly parts of the town like Alipasino Polje and some other parts of town. I don't know what the names are, but they can be seen with the naked eye, I was able to see very clearly the demarcation lines of Mount Igman. And also from the hospital, I was able to see the shelling of Ilidza, because it also could be seen from the second floor of the hospital. So apart from the knowledge I got from the patients where were wounded and how, but I was also to see with the naked eye from the hospital, and also I was moving about and I was there for a very long time in the firing areas of Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And from what you saw with your own eyes, Doctor, be it from the hospital or from around it or on those occasions when you moved around Sarajevo in the five districts that we are talking about, what can you tell us about the shelling frequency?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that shelling was very frequent. At times, there would be a shell or two. At times, there would be as many as a dozen. Several times during the period that we are talking about, as many as 100 shells would hit which means during more severe fighting because these separation lines went through various parts of the city, that is one part of the city fought against the other one. And they used all means of fighting in the struggle. I am saying this because I saw it and especially because of a high influx of the wounded, types of the wounds, and the case histories, that is, information we collected from the patients, the place, the time of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wounding, the place where a person was wounded, time, and whether that was a military or a civilian person. These are personal particulars which every doctor will seek from every patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Doctor, I am reading back your statement. You are telling us that you collected the information from patients when you were writing up their case histories. And you say that you also asked about the time and place of the -- these incidents. And what you were -- these information was, was it always included in the patient's case history, what kind of technique did you use to develop a patient's files?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is every doctor's duty to when admitting an injured or a sick person to get the particulars and the case history, especially in the case of an injured person whether it is at peacetime or war injury, it doesn't matter. One always records the time and place of every wounded. So for every wounded -- and this is tantamount to a law. So we also recorded the place where the person was wounded, the time, and the manner of wounding. And in this way, we had exact records, whether it was a military or a civilian person, and the place where the person had been wounded. This is very important to know because at a later stage in any court proceedings, be it the damages or whatever, it is important for the court also to know so as to be able to meet their request of the plaintiff or whatever it may be. We get cases of wounded who was self inflicted wounds, or those who got injured in a personal -- in brawls. So one had to be able to distinguish between such injuries and injuries sustained during fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. And now I would like to talk about patients and their ethnic background. What was, generally speaking, the procedure that you followed when and if soldiers were wounded and captured? Do you know something about that? I am talking only from the point of view of care.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to this question, I have to say, to begin with, that being a physician, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I shall try to be more precise. No, no, no. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot discriminate between patients on whatever grounds, be it national, religious or whatever. Physicians -- and I think that I am a patient -- at time a physician, and to us all patients equal, so that we treated equally all the patients regardless of their ethnic or religious background. Apart from it being a medical rule or rather that it is part of the doctor's ethics, this was also based on the requests of the political and military leadership of the Serb side that we applied a medical approach. I can give you two or three examples, and if you wish me, I could also explain in detail. I said yesterday that we had over 1.500 [Realtime transcript read in error"1.050"] --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am stopping you here. I am stopping you here. You said two examples because of the time. If you can give us these examples in just so many words, then we should be happy to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here 1.500. It is 150, not 1.000. So we had Croat and Muslims one dead soldier too. So I can give you the example of Croat soldiers, that is what I said. But perhaps it is more important to say that we treated Muslim soldiers. So I can give you the example of Mehmud Pustahija a Muslim soldier. He was from Visoko. He was a member of a unit from Visoko. He was an officer, but I wouldn't be able to tell you what his exact rank was, and he told us that he was -- he had been twice awarded the gold lily, which means that he was a twice time hero who entered our territory on a sabotage mission. And as we learned from military and civilian police sources in that area, he had liquidated seven Serb combatants. And as he was returning to his territory, he was ambushed, severely wounded, and had several bullets in his chest and abdomen, but he was brought in the hospital within one hour of the wounding because that is how far he was from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know that perhaps counsel has two hours and therefore he can use it. But could you explain the relevance of all of this to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The -- let me just try to focus your attention on two aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just before I give you an opportunity to respond, I will ask you to focus on two aspects. You did put a question to the witness what were the techniques used to -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Medical files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the witness took one minute and a half to tell us what the duty of a doctor is, and why it was important to register. He did not say anything about the techniques used. So that was one minute and a half. You didn't stop him, you just let him go. No, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me speak. Now, you are asking questions about whether any distinction was made in the medical treatment between, may I say, military or at least people from different ethnic background. And the answer seems to me quite clear that there was no distinction, and it is the duty of a doctor to treat a patient irrespective of what is. This last issue, Mr. Stamp asked what the relevance is. I am asking your attention as well for the first aspect I raised, that the witness took a lot of time without answering your question, without you intervening, and then finally, you went to the next question. Would you please explain what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be happy to do that. I will say this: I would like to when -- one examines very carefully what was my question in French, because I was not talking about medical techniques, but that is a detail. With regard to the relevance of this question, I will come to it, but before that, even before we lose time, I would like if the objection is not made to the question, but to the answer. And that is becoming a custom. But throughout, the relevance of this is as follows -- the relevance is as follows: The Prosecution indicated that there was a campaign intended to suppress, by all means available, civilians and military alike. And if there were such violations of the customs of war and Geneva Conventions, then, amongst the military, one could expect any one more drastic attitude because they are military, and therefore, they would not have done anything to save these people, they would have let them die or they would have left them to suffer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the relevance of your question depends on how we have to understand the Prosecution's case. Mr. Stamp, could you please tell us whether in the term "campaign" as it is used in the indictment, whether it is the case of the Prosecution that this would involve all sectors of -- I would say also civilian lives, such as doctors, medical treatment, that the campaign would implicate that soldiers of the other -- of the Sarajevo forces would not be treated medically on an equal footing as local patients?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is not an allegation of the Prosecution at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is not part of the Prosecution's case, please proceed to your next subject, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel switch on his microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, did you also treat civilians? I am not talking about military any longer, but about civilians, civilians who were not of Serb origin. What can you tell us briefly about that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I treated non-Serb civilians. Of course, there were many civilians, but the Croat and Muslim -- but more Croats than Muslim, quite so equally and without any difference whatsoever. So I treated both wounded and sick civilians -- I mean both. Civilians used to come from the municipalities I indicated where they lived, and from the municipalities of Kiseljak which was the municipality adjacent to Ilidza Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which was mostly inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, when fighting took place in the area that you were familiar with, were there any measures announcing them so as to protect the population?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about some two types of measures of announcement of protection; one was the siren announcing shelling. I can say this is something that I heard and saw with my own ears and eyes - this is personal experience - that people knew, when they heard the siren, from the other part of the city, that the siren in the part of the city controlled by Muslims, then Serb civilians and soldiers in the part controlled by the Serbs would immediately hide, because they knew that a few seconds after the siren in the Muslim part of the city, shells would start falling on the -- in the Serb part of the city. They knew that -- they knew that seconds or minutes later, Serb forces would be returning fire from Serb parts of the city against Muslim parts of the city, and that is how we knew the shells would be coming by hearing the sirens from the other side. I can only tell you that when there would be a larger number of shells, we always said that the first shell kills, because the first one comes as a surprise. People knew how to move, which parts of the city, on which side of the building, so that that was another protection on possible parts of the wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for being so concise. Now, I come back to the question of hospitals, Doctor. What can you tell us about the electricity, water, and the rest in hospitals or the hospital that you knew, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hospital that I worked in, we mostly used our generator. The generator, we used it more than the regular power supply. In these municipalities, again, there were power cuts, whether they had it more often than they didn't, I don't know. But they didn't have it often, and I can say that the same holds true of the city. Because the power supply from the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled by the Muslim forces would cross through the Serb part of the city and then go to the city. So the Serb forces could cut off the electricity in the part of the city inhabited by Muslims, but at the same time, perhaps half an hour, an hour later, the Muslim forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean Jablinica -- I can't remember exactly where, would cut off the power for the Serb part of the city. So it seemed to be on a reciprocal basis. Water was also a problem because when there was no electricity, there was no water. Heating was a serious problem, because the Serb part of the city mostly used gas that was -- there was a gas supply. I didn't know about that, because we don't have gas in Nis. And also traverse territories not controlled by the Serb forces or that gas by plant it was not always in working order. So that electricity water and gas were frequently the subject of haggling or bargaining between the two parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will move on to a different question, can you please tell us but once again very briefly first -- and we have to ask you to slow down. First, what can you tell us about the medicines, and medical supplies; and secondly, what can you tell us about the humanitarian aid in the areas in the region that you knew? Oh, yes, all right, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to try to be -- to slow down. The hospital -- the hospital supply was, as a rule, organised through humanitarian organisations. And I have to say to the French Battalion, French forces of the humanitarian organisations, I could mention Pharmaciens, Ca Frontier, the Croissant de Lune with Ca Frontier, the Red Cross and Red Crescent. Lots of supplies came from arabic countries. There were also some church humanitarian organisations, Caritas and I can't remember Adra or something. That accounted for 95 per cent of the supplies that hospital needed, medical supplies, I mean. Also, the United Nations forces, that is UNPROFOR as it was called then, also supplied hospitals with the medical supplies. It has been agreed that because the hospital was on the road that convoys had to cover to reach the part of the city controlled by the Muslims. So it was agreed that one-third of the medical supplies should be left with our hospital, and two-thirds could be taken to the Kosevo Hospital, which was a regular hospital in another part of the city. And the United Nations forces respected that agreement. That is how we both got our supplies. However, there were frequent problems with that. At times, they would forget about us. At times, we would get something that we did not need, for instance, some supplies for cardiographic treatment which is something which we did not need but I guess those were errors. I don't think such errors were done deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I am going to interrupt you now. Thank you very much. When we talk about medical supplies for hospital, there is more to it than medical supplies. There are also some aids, such as for instance, oxygen bottles and so on and so forth. Where did this come from, this is my first question? And what can you tell us on the subject, but very briefly? And I will interrupt you when necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These auxiliary equipment came from the world over. It went through the part of the city controlled by the Serb forces and went onto the part controlled by the Muslim forces. On one occasion, we needed oxygen and nitrogen, two gases which are necessary for general anesthesia. We could not make it because this is medical oxygen, not industrial oxygen. We were getting it from Kiseljak, but where from, I don't know. I am not sure it was not done or packed in Kiseljak. It must have been coming from some other place, be it Bosnia-Herzegovina or somewhere, I don't know. But over 15 bottles we received five and ten went on to the city.
