utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us, please: Why was this hospital established where it was, the one that you worked in? Why was it there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This hospital was founded in a part of the city, in the Serb part of the city, because it was the only hospital accessible to the population of that part of the city, and those military. That is the nearest hospital from the beginning from May to August when I wasn't there, but I know that. There was the Kasindol Hospital and it took half an hour to reach it. One would have to go to the Butmir airport runway when the airport was turned over to UNPROFOR forces when the Serbs that is lost control over that runway. The Muslim forces came next to the runway on both sides, and I could see it because I went there. They were on the very edge of the runway so that any further transport using the runway was impossible. And in the early days we were trying to use ambulance cars, but they were shot at. And they transported to the hospital in Pale, the next nearest hospital called Koran on the northern edge of Sarajevo, and it took five or six hours to get there. There was no road there. It had been barely made, dug, in order to connect the part of the city controlled by the Serbs which was closed from all sides accept this very narrow road which provided -- Pale, and it took six hours to get there crossing fields and going over a dirt road. So this was too critical for the wounded. Because in the case of severe wounds, such long-lasting transport, especially if they were bleeding and lethally, so that was they reached Pale either dead or in very severe Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. traumatic or hemorrhagic shock. So the fatality until the surgical unit was opened in the town, the fatality reached 70 or even 80 per cent which is a horrific fact at the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You spoke to us about digging through this road. Now, I have two -- no, three questions. The first one is: What was the duration, the time which was necessary to get to the hospital in the part of the city which is called Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you meant Pale, not Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I know. But I am asking you a question --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. It took about four to six hours to Pale, plus about two hours to Grbavica. So eight hours altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question concerning Grbavica: What can you tell us about the way in which this area lived, that is, could one enter it freely? Was it turned into an enclave or what?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I visited Grbavica only once. And I can say that it took me so about 4 to 6 hours to Pale and 2 more to Grbavica, and it was very difficult because it was a narrow road behind Trebevic from Pale to Grbavica. It was a very difficult round about way to get there. If I told you that it is 15 minutes from Ilidza to Grbavica to go to the city, then you will understand what the means to travel eight hours around the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, we are talking about roads and routes. Did you see, with your own eyes, to walk on foot in the city where you worked, how did people walk in, that is, moving on foot, protect themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I also moved around pass the city, I knew from my own experience where I could go and where I couldn't. Not only the adults, children knew that too. For instance, there was some intersections which were open in Ilidza, in Vogosca, in Hadzici, these were quite open, exposed, to parts of the city held by Muslim forces. And one could not use those intersections. I am talking about urban intersections. One could not go through them which would have been the shortcut. That is, you couldn't cross the street. You had to go around the building or take some other route in order not to become the target for a possible rifle from the other side. Also, some streets, for instance, Kasindolska Street in Ilidza, but there were a number of others too, they were exposed to infantry fire. I cannot say "sniper fire" because I do not know if it is a sniper bullet or ordinary one, that is, whether one used sights or just the naked eye. Because it could be either very near or it could be very far. But some streets, such as Kasindolska, were wide open --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, I will stop you here. Thank you. We have understood that there were areas which were exposed. But in areas which you could see, were there, or perhaps were there not some special systems of protection against such attacks, against these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were very specific system, and I came across them for the first time. Before that, I never saw them, even on film. And those were sheets, sheets of cloth or cardboard shields. They would be stretched across the streets, and on the sides, one could have large pieces of cardboard or paper so that the pedestrians moving there could be protected from being seen from either side, and thereby from possible shots at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Doctor, you have just mentioned the term "sniper." A doctor, can he or can he not, when he see as bullet wound, say technically whether it was a sniper bullet or perhaps some other kind of bullet wound?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear that a physician can never say whether a bullet came from a sniper or not. A physician, a surgeon, can know clearly whether a wound had been inflicted by an infantry weapon, but whether it was a sniper or not, he has no way of knowing. Because the only difference can be the depth of the wound. And a good marksman can hit from a thousand to 1500 metres, but you cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doctor, can a physician make a difference when he is dealing with a bullet wound, whether it was a direct hit or a ricochet hit, whether it was a direct wound or a wound which was the result of a ricochet? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course one can. There is a major difference between a direct hit and a ricochet. Do you want me to explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I do not think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber would like to hear a short explanation of what -- how this difference can be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Direct hit, whether it was small calibre ammunition or conventional ammunition, that is, .556 is small, or .79, the conventional ammunition, both types of bullets, both types of projectiles were used in the war in Sarajevo. A direct hit will produce a clear, round, small wound at the entry, and at the exit also slightly larger, but round. Whereas, the ricochet will produce an irregularly shaped wound and on both sides the skin will be scorched and the circle will be regular. Why? Because a bullet if we take a small calibre, 5.56 [as interpreted], such a bullet travels because the bullet, projectile, .556 travels faster than 1200 metres per second, its velocity is very high. It has a tremendous kinetic energy, but small mess. Therefore, its entry will be narrow and the wound inside will be large. Whereas a ricochet, when the bullet has ricochetted from a wall, floor, asphalt loses the velocity suddenly. The bullet doesn't rotate regularly around its axis, but irregularly so that it lacerates the skin, the subcutaneous tissue, and produce as large wound. So that the difference is quite clear, that is, insofar as infantry weapons are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And, therefore, Doctor, in the light of what you have just told us when you are issued a medical document or are preparing a medical document, is it that you could always -- that you couldn't put a sniper bullet, because you didn't know that, you couldn't know that technically whether it was a sniper bullet or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All that we put in is -- well, we put it in Latin. But we merely said whether it was a bullet wound, that is, a sclopetarium or a wound inflicted by an infantry weapon, or an explosive wound caused by artillery weapon. But we, as physicians, cannot say whether it was a sniper bullet or not. It can be perhaps done by those who conduct investigations or other competent agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I am now going back to another series of questions. You spoke to us about the locality of Grbavica. You told us that it was difficult to get there. Was it as difficult to leave it, that is, whether people who lived there, from what you know, were in a way - in a manner of speaking - imprisoned in Grbavica for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how one entered Grbavica, and that was also the only way to get out of Grbavica. I told you it was very hard. And many times during the first month of my stay there -- because it was in November that I arrived in Sarajevo -- and between the 4th of October until November, I was in Pale at the Koran Hospital where wounded from Grbavica came. And oftentimes, I came across a situation, that is more than ten times during that month, when wounded members, that is, members of wounded combatants from Grbavica when they came, that their relatives coming to visit their wounded members of family wounded combatants at Pale would be wounded or even killed on the way from Grbavica to Pale, so that this route was taken only when you had no other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation, please -- what was the situation concerning other areas that you knew, and I mean Ilidza, Vogosca, Hadzic, and others?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those localities were exposed equally to infantry and artillery fire. And there was a rule amongst the population that movement is highly dangerous. One moved about only when one had to and in special situations. So that any movement was dangerous than being in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my last -- two last questions. You said that you saw with your own eyes those two oxygen bottles a moment ago. To your knowledge -- to your knowledge, were there similar instances, that is, when weapons were found in some pretty strange place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw those bottles and all that. Apart from that, the only thing I know also is -- and it also happened en route to the part of the city controlled by the Muslim forces -- when a trailer was intercepted and when the container was lifted, in the trailer itself, 40 to 50.000 machine-gun, Browning machine-gun bullets were found. I just happen to be in the part of the city when that happened. And I -- later on, I also saw it on television. And international forces which were there at the time are also aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what was the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime perhaps in mid-1993. I can't give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know what was that convoy? Was it a private convoy or was it some other kind of convoy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it had United Nations markings, but I am not 100 per cent sure, but it can be checked, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Stamp, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you mobilised at any time for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, because I am a national of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How does this kind of question relate to the province of relevance? How is this brigade relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness here has testified that he is a volunteer. I think we are entitled to inquire of the witness in cross-examination about his background and anything that he might have participated in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when I just said something to Mr. Stamp about objections, I think urged the parties because the background of the witness is -- has only been the subject of cross-examination by the Defence. Civilians were always examined thoroughly on, I would say, military presence in the third degree and the families, so this type of question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- May I so simply to ask you if you should intervene? I don't have always the English channel in my ears, and at times I am covered by what you are saying. Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You first volunteered to work in Knin, in the Krajina in 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from there, you moved on to the Sarajevo opstina?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at any time were you posted to work, as a doctor with the Zvornik Brigade or any brigade in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never worked, and I have only passed through Zvornik once in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you at any time work as a doctor with the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You gave us some figures for persons you said were injured. Were those persons persons who were treated in your hospital at Zica? Or may I put it this way: Persons that were treated at the Zica hospital that you worked at?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you only figures for the hospital that I worked for in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that the Zica hospital? Was that known as the Zica hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is what it was called after a facility. Before the war, it was a recreation home near Sarajevo, the hospital was put up there. But people continued to call it Zica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. And that was in a place called Blazuj or something sounding like that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is at the municipality of Ilidza at the very entrance of the Blazuj locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the figures you gave us they were the figures for wounded persons between 1992 to 1995 during the war? Or was it 1996?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures covered a period from the 1st of November 1992 to 1st of February 1996. That is until the last day I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to hand you a map, a blank map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Unhappily, Mr. President, we only have one copy of this blank map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it could be put on the ELMO we can use it. But would you please take care next time that there are sufficient maps available. At least if you need the witness to do some markings, otherwise, we have the blank map as such as has been admitted into evidence, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P3274. And perhaps it would be P3274ML. I asked the witness to mark the map. I think that map has been used before in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is, Mr. Stamp, that usually the Judges and the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would copy their own markings on their own copy of the map and it is impossible now. It is highly inconvenient the way you are dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the Defence would also like to have a copy of this. I see that it is a large map. It will be impossible to have it whole on the ELMO, not the whole Sarajevo. So would Mr. Stamp please be so kind to supply us with one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map as such, I take it, is admitted in the evidence, so you have a copy of that. But it is highly inconvenient that Mr. Stamp did not provide us with extra copies. Mr. Stamp, would it be possible to provide us after the next break with a copy or if that would be -- is there a possibility? I don't know how important it is in your line of questioning to deal with these matters right away or that you can do it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I could try to get copies and deal with it at a later stage -- of the maps. The reason why I have decided to use this map arose out of the cross-examination [sic] and something I heard this morning, so I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The examination-in-chief, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The examination-in-chief, I beg your pardon. We are making efforts to locate the copies. Perhaps some are in stock and would produce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were referring to 3724, because that is a map which is at least a look-alike from what I see from a distance. 3274 Madam Registrar informs me is photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3724 is what the Registry tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have 3274 marked on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, it is possible to get the original ones? Please proceed. We will check meanwhile with some other subjects so that we can return to it after we have checked what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A tape was played which we all saw. Were you the doctor on that tape?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not the doctor. That was Dr. Pejic who is a specialist of ear, nose, and throat. He is the head of the hospital. Myself, as a surgeon, I did not speak to the journalist. I did not give a statement to the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you present when that tape was made?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present when the bottles were brought, when they were opened, but while the interview was being done, I was in the surgery, because some injuries -- injured patients were brought. And I watched how the television interview was proceeding. So throughout the time, I was in the courtyard of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And now, I just wish to move on to the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp, it is not the fault of the Chamber of the Defence that we have no copies. If we want to follow any markings on the map, we should have a map in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be clear, otherwise we are working on maps without the markings on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that, however, sometimes these things to arise and we are making efforts to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you -- I don't know whether many markings have to be made, but perhaps we could leave the -- and apart from that, Mr. Stamp, in evidence is under number 3274A, 3274B, and 3274C, three photographs. If I may just refer to them, these are photographs related to victims in a bus, if that sounds familiar to you. Under 3724, a map is admitted into evidence; that is a blank map. So I take it that you want to present to the witness a map, that should be at the number of 3724 and then the initials of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps, if you have no other questions, perhaps you start and we will see where we have difficulties in following the markings. If it is just one marking, it is of course different from if you want five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to ask you to mark on the map where the hospital was located --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, we agreed, the Defence and the Prosecution and the Chamber accepted this that throughout the examination of a witness, either by Prosecution or the Defence, we would be using the map P3644. I believe this is the map that was shown to all the witnesses. And then apart from -- then we would put next to P3644, we would put the initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't that the map of the city while this is a map of a wider area? We have the big black and white map, that is 3724. And I think the other map is the map with the names of the streets on it, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did not receive the map beforehand. We don't know whether this is a map of a wider area or it is a city map. Perhaps we could have a closer look at it and we would be able to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will show you 3724 -- no, am I right -- yes, 3724. I get confused myself. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stamp and we will see where we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, could you please mark on that map the location of the Zica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am to mark the place -- I don't have any experience with maps --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. But the methodology that we have used has always been the same. Every time that the witness has to mark something, we mark it on our own maps so that we know about it afterwards. When the debriefing goes on, we can see what happened. Now, we can't do it because they refuse to give us a map. I don't think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not use strong words like "refuse." Let's just put the map on the ELMO and see whether the marking as requested by the Prosecution can be made on this map. Would you perhaps indicate, Doctor, the area of the map where the hospital was located so that we can all see it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that this is my very first experience with a map of this area. But through the names, perhaps I would be able to tell -- I don't know what the ratio -- what the scale of the map is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from scale of maps or not, I think this is not the map we just mentioned. I would like to see the map that is presented to the witness at this very moment. It is the map that was exceptionally used. It is not the ordinary black and white one we often use, but it is the map used during the examination of Witness AD, as far as I can see. So could that part we placed on the ELMO so that everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In order to make it a little easier for you, Witness, could you find on the map where Blazuj is? Have you seen it? Can you put a circle around Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to find everything on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around Blazuj now, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a blue marker? Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you put a dot there. What does that dot indicate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dot indicates the area where the hospital was located. As orientation, I used the road which goes to the -- towards the place of Osijek, where there is an underpass. And the hospital was just behind this road next to the church. So just by the road, there is the church and the hospital. So I think that it is a good orientation. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether or not to the south of where that hospital was there was a confrontation line between the VRS and the ABiH and how far it was. I am not asking you to mark anything now. I am asking you to tell us whether or not you knew there was a line to the south of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what's the south is. Is it this down here towards me or is it up there? South in relation to the city, if you can just tell me what the southern side is, I can tell you. I can tell you on all four sides, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Take your eyes off the map for a minute. I just want to ask you a couple of questions. The position of your hospital from Alipasino Polje was about 7 kilometres. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is 7 kilometres, but I think I know what you mean. It is possible to see Alipasino Polje from the hospital, for sure. You can check this. These are skyscrapers. These are the only skyscrapers. It is possible to see, that is what I said earlier. It is possible to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's get back to the question. You are saying that you can't answer whether or not the distance between your hospital and Alipasino Polje would be about 7 kilometres? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me, I don't know. But do you mean as the crow flies or on the road? You are asking me if you can see it. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. We will get to that later. If you listen to my questions first and answer those. As the crow flies, you wouldn't be able to say whether it is about 7 kilometers or more? More in the region of 8 kilometers? If you can't say, you can't say.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you correctly whether it is 7 kilometers. Perhaps it is 5, perhaps it is 7. I don't know, I really don't know. I could explain to you how long it would take by road, as you take it car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Lazic, you told us that you couldn't tell us exact distance. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Since we didn't have time to look at the map beforehand, you know that I am not a specialist, would it be possible to ask about the scale so that we could find our bearings. Could Mr. Stamp tell us because I don't think I can see what the scale of the map is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the witness doesn't know anything of the distance. Let's deal with the scale at a later moment, because this was a question not related to the map. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed just to say that it might assist the court that we have evidence about the scale of this map from Witness AD, so we could look to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Between the hospital and Alipasino Polje, there are a few built up communities including Otes and Nedzarici. Is that correct? I beg your pardon, Otes and Nedzarici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Between the hospital and Alipasino Polje, in my opinion, there is only one locality, Dogladi and Azici. This is a locality with only Dogladi, and Azici is only low houses, no high-rises. Alipasino Polje is -- has nothing -- Alipasino Polje and the hospital only have low houses between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: As the crow flies, would you say that the community of Nedzarici is between where the hospital was and Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzarici is located in this area, but not as you look towards the Alipasino Polje settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that Hadzici and Ilijas were also part of Sarajevo from which you took casualties. Is that fair? Could you put a circle around Hadzici where it is.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you put a circle, a circle and a cross around Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you find Kiseljak on this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, may I just return to Ilijas. You asked to make a circle and a cross. Dr. Lazic, could you on Ilijas, please, add a cross to the circle. Yes, that is Kiseljak. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The circle at Ilijas, you have put a cross and circle. You have also put a cross and a circle at Kiseljak. For the Ilijas, could you just put a figure "1" beside that circle and the cross at Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three. I have marked there three. And Ilijas and Kiseljak, and before that Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, now, Ilijas is a circle and a cross, and a "1." Kiseljak is now a circle and a cross where -- no, no, you don't have to add -- please, please. And just a circle was the first marking made. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we -- can you just assume for the sake of the next few questions that Hadzici is to the east of Blazuj -- sorry -- to the west of Blazuj, and Ilijas to the north, so you can get your -- good. Do you know where the lines were to the east of Hadzici where the confrontation line -- sorry -- to the west of Hadzici. Do you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Hadzici is to the west. The confrontation line west from Hadzici was located exactly on the edge of the locality towards the west. I don't know the localities themselves. I don't know them because they are on the other side of the demarcation line. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But approximately to the west, to the edge of that circle that you put for Hadzici. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it should be. I can't guarantee you 100 per cent. By the localities and by the map, it is west on the very edge. I am not an expert for maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are now going into detail, very precise detail, on the positions of the lines. I believe it is absolutely indispensable to have the maps so that we can reproduce the markings on the document, otherwise we are not going to be able to proceed later on. And we are not going to be able to ensure the proper defence of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you have any idea how much time it would take still to provide us with the maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have just received information. It is going to be impossible to provide maps, copies of these maps today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have the marked maps reproduced at a later stage so that the Defence has a -- even a better copy of the map with the markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it that care will be taken that the mark -- the maps as they are marked will be given to the Defence once being copied. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am wondering if the Defence has copy of the one which was used with Witness AD. Perhaps if they do, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We should not ask the Defence to mark a marked map, because it would lose its quality of a copy of the -- of the exhibit admitted in the evidence. So that is not a solution, I think, Mr. Stamp. The Defence will be provided with a copy of the marked map in a later stage. And at this moment we have the original of the marked map available, so that if any additional question would arise, that we can use this map. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, to the south of Blazuj - and remember Ilijas is to the north and the south is opposite to the north - would you agree with me that the confrontation lines in that direction were about 1 to 2 kilometres away from Blazuj? You have to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Lazic, nodding is a bit difficult for the interpreters to translate. And on our transcript, we need your response. Yes, so would you please speak aloud instead of nodding. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just waiting for the interpretation to finish. I was nodding for the -- before the end of the interpretation. Yes, I fully agree with you, yes. Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And according to you, there was a lot of fighting in the Igman area. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You took casualties from all of these areas in Sarajevo, as you know it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In all the municipalities, in all the area between these municipalities. So that was all the area between the demarcation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, the confrontation lines to the north of that circle that you put at Ilijas was about a kilometre away. Is that correct? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the hospital to Ilijas, that is what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. The lines of confrontation between the two warring sides, to the north of Ilijas, the circle for Ilijas, was approximately a kilometre away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel wait until the end of the interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Let me have a look. Yes, approximately, yes, that is approximately right, from Pogluvi as far as I know, Pogluvi was also in the Serb area and further on it is on an irregular line. But, yes, that is what you can say. I do not know exactly on the map. It is not a straight line. For instance, the village that I can't see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to check on something that Prosecution said earlier; it is about the objection. I am objecting to this because the competencies of the witness is not of a military of someone who was a soldier in the field and asking him to localise this on such a map as this, I don't think that that is proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You agree that -- without looking at the map -- you said that you knew where battles were fought and combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please respond to the objection, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. The objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was about the beyond the competence of this witness to say anything about the localities -- he is not a military and therefore could not identify confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness in chief gave a lot of evidence about combats in this zone that his hospital covered from which they took patients, they took casualties. And he spoke of knowing about it, firstly. So I submit that the question is alleged to my question, if he cannot answer, he cannot. Secondly, the objection does not address a question. All I asked the witness was simply if he can say whether or not the confrontation line to the north of Ilijas is approximately a kilometre away from where he put the circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can answer that question, you may do so. The objection is denied. But, of course, if you don't know, you can't tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness did answer, but perhaps you could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I missed that answer, because I was about to give a decision on the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the answer does not appear in the transcript. Could you please repeat the answer to the question of Mr. Stamp. Could you please repeat the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say whether or not the confrontation lines to the north of Ilijas, that is where you put the circle with the number "1" on the map, was approximately a kilometre away from Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Yes, one kilometre is possible. But what I can say also is that I know very well that the area and confrontation line toward the city. I did not visit the confrontation lines along the outer ring, because it is a mountainous area, and I didn't go there. But I know it was quite near Ilijas, perhaps a kilometre or two. I know how the lines went towards the city. And I know almost every place there toward city, but outside along this outer ring, I mean, it is 10, 20 kilometers, over the mountains. And I really do not know which direction it took, except some places, Igman, Zuc, from where the shelling came. Other things I can make guesses. Outer ring, as we would call it

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Lazic, may I ask you to listen carefully to the questions and answer that question. The question was: Whether the confrontation line was how much north from Ilijas. If counsel for the Prosecution would like to know whether you have any further knowledge of the confrontation lines, he will certainly ask you. But we are under some time restraints. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said shelling came from Igman, Mount Igman. Was that where the major part of the shelling came from into your area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area where the hospital was, Ilidza, the municipality of Ilidza, yes, most shells came from Igman. Some came from the city, but from Igman, yes, that is where the majority of shells came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you consider Igman a part of Sarajevo, by your definition of what Sarajevo is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I do not know whether Mount Igman is legally part of the municipality of Sarajevo. I didn't give you my definition. I told you about what Sarajevo looked before the war, at that time I knew which were the municipalities of Sarajevo. And that was a decision taken by the city. That was not something that I invented. And how the city was built and organised, that is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. The answer is you don't know whether it is legally a part of Sarajevo. You saw skyscrapers in Alipasino Polje from the second floor of the hospital in Zuc [sic]; that is your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I make it -- you mean Blazuj and not Zuc?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, that is what I was about to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You could see the top of those skyscrapers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of the skyscrapers. I don't know if there were 10-, 12-storey high, and then I would see two or three floors, and then at times I saw the whole body of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The urban part of the city of Sarajevo, that part which was controlled by the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you visit that part between the 10th of September 1992 to the 10th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection in principle. Because the questions, as it was phrased, implies the idea of a city, but city only which is in the hands of the Federation. Because the question begins, "The urban part of the city of Sarajevo," as if other parts were not also urban parts. And I think that a distinction is drawn here implied by the question. The Defence wishes the question to be reworded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand the question to be whether you ever visited those parts of the city that were under control by the BiH forces. Is that correct, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may then answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Between August -- between September 1992 and August 1994, in that time period.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you were not on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am sorry. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Dr. Lazic, the Judges have a few questions for you as well, but perhaps first the Defence -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am sorry, but so that we can see whether there are some other questions, I need the map to have a look at it. I am really sorry, but that is not the Defence's fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is perhaps one question -- [In English] Do not fold it. Okay. [Interpretation] There is one question which we could ask in relation to the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do so if you -- if that comes out from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes. Because the question was about the exact position of the hospital. That we wanted to show how difficult it was, we want the witness to mark with a different pen the route which one had to take before the hospital in order to get from this neighbourhood in the east to the area of Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is my recollection well that it was a specific -- it was during the examination-in-chief that the difficulty road to Pale was explained by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the opinion that although perhaps the question does not directly relate to the examination-in-chief -- to the cross-examination, that it might be of assistance to the Chamber to have this route marked on the map. So unless -- well, let's see how -- whether and how quick it can be done. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President we shall ask the witness to do it, but we wanted first to examine the whole map in order to avoid errors, and only when he is quite certain that he knows the route to take a pen of different colour, I believe, that will be black, on it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just be very practical. To do it with some precision, that might take some time. Could it not be done in the presence of both parties during the break under the supervision of a -- and that we then see the result after the break? I am aware, Dr. Lazic, that I might deprive you from a cup of coffee but perhaps -- if that would be -- so we will do that during the break and first see perhaps whether there are any other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Mr. President. Because since we shall save time in this manner, let me have 30 seconds to tell you why we consider the relevant and important. It would be of use to the Chamber and perhaps the Prosecution simply to show that before this hospital was set up there, one needed an amount of time to get to the hospital, and that was why the hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Relevance is not in dispute. You asked the witness to marked the road -- the route, and he will do so during the break. If this was your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Judges have some questions for you as well. Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Doctor, you said that as a physician, you don't know whether a wound was produced or provoked by a sniper bullet or a bullet coming from other infantry weapons. What is, for you, a "sniper"? What is your understanding of a "sniper"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: A bullet from infantry weapons -- infantry weapons, I can give you two examples. The rifle used by the former Yugoslav People's Army and that was 7.9 calibre, and it was used by both sides in the early days of the war. Or some American rifles of small calibres, if they have optical sights and use the sights to target it, and you need sights to target something that is further away, that is a sniper. If you fire without such sights, that is a shorter distances, these are wounds inflicted by infantry weapons. So the weapons are the same, except that in one case you use sights and in others not. Now, whether he was lying somewhere and waiting or whether he simply fired blindly towards the locality and hit somebody, we, the physicians, cannot say that. All we can say is that it was wound inflicted by infantry weapons or by artillery weapons and we can say whether we are dealing with small-calibre ammunition or conventional ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Doctor, I would like to go back to what you said about the experience that you had in treating the wounded from the other side. I am referring to other parties to the conflict. And you said that you were a humanist and that the medical ethics was imperative for you and you did what you had to do. But in your testimony you also said that there were certain instructions coming from the military and the civilians to the fact that you - being in the hospital, a doctor - had to treat, had to attend to all of the ethnicities or all the ethnic groups in Bosnian. I would like you to tell me a little bit more about those instructions, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. Those were not really instructions. Those were mostly conversations. Because a number of military and political leaders visited the hospital, visiting the wounded, from Corps Commanders, army commanders to municipality mayors. And whenever they visited the wounded, the hospital, they extended the same kind of attention to Serb ethnicities and other ethnicities. And never forgot to point out, when talking to doctors, that it was very important, and that it was very highly necessary for us to comply by the Physician's Oath and to attend to all wounded. Otherwise, they issued no instructions, no directions or anything. They merely pointed out what was our duty and that was how it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Doctor, can you tell us if you remember the names of some of these military or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those who visited the hospital? Well, for instance, the -- yes. That's right. The mayor of the municipality of Ilidza, I can't remember him. General Galic, corps commander. Commander of another brigade, Mr. Krajisnik, came -- I can't remember them all because there were many. The minister of health care Mr. Kalinic. So prominent figures came to visit the wounded. And I think that it is their duty. I think it would be horrible, if leaders, especially military leaders, didn't come to visit their wounded. The hospital was in the city itself. And whenever they came, they always spoke about and always pointed out the humaneness of the Serb side. And as far as I know, the same holds true on the other side as far as medical is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to General Galic, did he mention this once? Twice? If I remember well, you went -- you arrived in that hospital in November, that is when you started working there in 1992. Can we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you stayed there until 1996. But what I am interested in is from the period from the time when you arrived until, say, August or September 1994. Do you remember, did General Galic come once or several times? Did he talk with you or with all of the hospital staff? Could you please shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic, as the Corps Commander, that is what he was called, Sarajevo Romanija Corps, which covered that area there -- a broader area, he came five or six times, that is, several times to visit the wounded. He talked with them. He also talked with the hospital staff during the visit. At times he would stay half an hour, at times a little longer. But generally speaking, he talked both with the wounded and the personnel about the problems we came across, whether we had problems with medical supplies, did the wounded have some complaints, as is due after all. He did what a military commander will do when he comes to visit a hospital. But he took care of the operation of the hospital and the health care of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, to understand you better, do I understand your directives, instructions, to attend to everybody irrespective of their ethnicity? It is this particular point that I would like you to concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am concentrated. I am saying there were no directives, no instructions. But he always emphasised a wonderful example of the doctors who treated everybody regardless. He emphasised this as a paramount of humaneness and the Serb attitude towards the war, I mean, with regard to the medical profession. I don't know anything outside that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Lazic, I have got a few questions for you as well. You explained to us how the long journey to Pale would create a risk that patients already died by reaching Pale. Could you tell us: Why were they transported to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From May 1992, in May 1992, a hospital was established, but it had no general surgeons. That the surgeons who could operate on the chest, abdomen, and large blood vessels. They had an orthopedic surgeon who could operate bones. They had specialists for ear, nose, and throat, otorhinolaryngologist, but they didn't have a surgeon and they didn't have an anesthesiologist. All of the wounded necessitating urgent operations, chest, abdomen, large blood vessels, extremities, and the body, had to be surgically treated if they were to survive. Since there were no surgeons or the operation theatre or anything, they were transported to Pale. And it took four or six hours. They were transported in a vehicle which is called 150. It was a lorry which belonged to the former Yugoslav People's Army with four bunks, as in a train, suspended, and they had a nurse with them. Such patients, when I was in Pale in October, I was there to admit such a lorry every night because, of course, they had not travelled by day. They did it at night. So of the four or five wounded transported, one of them would be lying on the floor. And I have to tell you, if somebody had -- was wounded at 2 or 3.00, he had to wait for the night to fall to be transported, that is, you were not transported immediately. So when they arrived there, one or two were already dead and the rest were in shock. That is the only reason for the transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still try to understand you. You say that certain facilities are not available in Pale like physicians and general surgeons, is that a correct understanding? Or is it just the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the other way around downhill, down in Sarajevo there were none and there were some in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So patients that needed general surgery for which the facilities were not in your hospital to be transported to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying, if it was a hospital which worked on the 1st of November until I came, there were no general surgeons there. So that all the patient whose needed surgical treatment went to Pale. On the 1st of November, I came down from Pale with the anesthetist, the assistant, and that is when we started an operation theatre in the kitchen of that recreation home and that is when we started an operating theatre in the kitchen of that new creation home, and that is when we started operating on patients in the hospital that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the situation you just described is the situation that existed before you arrived in the hospital where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have also indicated to us how far it was to Grbavica. Would patients from Grbavica, would they be transported for treatment and surgery to Pale or to your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to Pale, naturally, because it took an hour and a half to two hours, perhaps, to get to Pale. So they were taken to Pale only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear to me. Then I have a -- you told us about the, I would say, the documentary part of your profession, that is, records kept in view of patients. Are they still available? Because you told us about it, but we haven't seen any of these medical records.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All medical institutions in the world over medical records are kept in the hospital. Not even an X-ray can leave the hospital. And the patients are issued with a discharge document, and it includes a diagnoses in Latin, the Latin description of the operation undertaken. And in the local language, you have further explanation, what kind of the problem we were treating, what was done, when the patient left, whether he needs to come for checkups or not. So this is the only document the patient is issued with, and his case history remains in the hospital, the records remain in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down although the interpreters do a perfect job in following you, but it is very difficult. Are all these documents still available in this hospital where you worked, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: On the 1st of February, 1996, the hospital shut down -- no a little bit before that. I left on the 1st of February. So I think that on the 20th of February. Because under Dayton, that part of Sarajevo was reunite would another part and that hospital was shut down. So that all the medical records were transferred to the Kasindol Hospital, which is still a legal hospital, a lawful hospital, because it was a lawful hospital just before the war. So all the medical records I believe can be found at the Kasindol. I kept my personal records and I have over 50 papers which I published at home and abroad with slides, over 500 slides. More than 50 hours are on tape so that if you wish me, I can send you some of my documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If needed, we might ask you to do so. Then I have some questions about the oxygen bottles. You told us that you were present during the interview of Dr. Pejic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment I was in the infirmary, that is, I was there, I went into the infirmary for two or three minutes. The whole thing took two or three hours until relevant officers came to establish what it was. This whole incident lasted two hours, not less than that, and I was there all the time and went in the infirmary for a couple of minutes. The anesthetist who discovered them determined the weight, he is called is Misur, you can also inquire if need be, and he can also tell you something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will ask you specific questions about that. Have you seen Dr. Pejic being interviewed? Did you see that or were you in at that moment? Were you inside? Were you close to it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview last said about five minutes. I saw part of it, not the whole of it. But I saw him stand there and talk and I think that the cameraman was Spomejika Durdevic, I mean that was the interviewer, Spomejika Durdevic, that was the name of the interviewer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We saw it on the video as the oxygen bottles being opened at the bottom after the interview. Was that the following order you noticed or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bottle -- the oxygen bottle were unscrewed in the presence of international forces prior to the interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was: Was this before or after the interview of Dr. Pejic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard Dr. Pejic say that the two bottles, he was using the plural, that they were filled with gunpowder, which surprises me if I compare that to the pictures I saw and to your testimony. Have you any possible explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing which is correct is that there were two bottles, that one of them contained gunpowder and the other one detonators. I suppose if you went through the whole tape, you would also see the other bottle with gunpowder. Whether Dr. Pejic -- whether it was a slip of the tongue on Dr. Pejic's part or something, I do not know. But I am quite certain that one of the bottles contained gunpowder and the other one the detonators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Dr. Pejic gave -- yes, Dr. Pejic also gave an explanation for the suspicion. He said: "Initially we thought that there was water inside or something else that froze because the weather was extremely cold. However, even after we thawed them, the cylinders were as heavy as before. We then decided to call in technicians," and then he continues. Were you present when this suspicion came up? So in the stage where there was suspicions about the weight of the bottles?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present personally, and the anesthetist contacted me first and said, I don't know what is going on, the bottles are unusually weighty, heavy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you thawed them up and they were still as heavy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then all of us in the hospital, we gathered and the chief came as well, and he wasn't there at the time. And then he came and then there was suspicion that this was something that was frozen, that this was a gas that was frozen inside. So we called him to find out, but before the bottles were opened, we asked all of the people to come there, all the people in authority, international officials. And then the bottles were opened after that. But there was suspicion that this was frozen gas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Pejic says that they were then thawed up and that they were just as heavy as before, and that you then decided to call in technicians. Is that your recollection as well, or would you have a different recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. But certainly we wouldn't have think -- thought of warming the bottles up; that is for sure. Let me tell you something: Because in Rajlovac in the vicinity, there was some oxygen factory which was making technical gas, not the one that can be used for -- in anesthetics. So somebody did come and say, Why don't we warm it up? But, of course, we didn't do it. I think somebody had suggested that, but because the bottle was still heavy, then military experts were called to see what was going on. I can tell you that there was this white -- this blue band at the very end of the bottle. When somebody took that band off, then we can see there was a bottle line of the cut, and this blue tape band covered this line. When the band or the tape came off, then we could see that there was a line, the bottle had been cut and somebody said, Let's unscrew it to see what's inside. I can't tell you any more details t was a long time ago. But this is a very interesting thing that happened, and hard to forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you studied medicine, may I take it that you are familiar with the basics of physics?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did make you expect that an iron bottle with a frozen liquid in it would be heavier or lighter than the same bottle with the same content of not frozen liquid?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told by the anesthesia technicians who worked with the equipment for anesthesiology and he worked for 10 years, and he told us that this was too heavy. So that this is where our suspicion came from, otherwise we didn't really think as to its physics, but he said he saw that from his experience, he thought maybe it was frozen gas. That was the idea. So it was the anesthetist -- the person who assists the anesthesiologist, the doctor, and he is the one who is in charge of all the equipment, the bottles, screwing them in, in screwing them, and so on, and that's what he said. It's on the basis of what he said that we had our suspicions. At the time, nobody thought about the laws of physics at the time. It was such time that nobody thought that something else could be in -- we never thought that in regular bottles of oxygen that would be something else. It was just logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if there would have been liquid oxygen in it, would it have a different weight in frozen or in liquid form?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, I am afraid. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Since you -- yes, Mr. Stamp. Is there any -- I have to look at whether we should have a break because we have late already, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My question is very, very brief. Just the date of this event that he was asked about, if he can tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that is in the general interest. Do you remember the date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened sometime -- I can't tell you the exact date, but it was end of January, beginning of February 1993, end of January beginning of February. It was around that time. I can't tell you the exact day. It was winter, but it was a fine day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only have two questions that stem only from the questions of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all to keep in mind that the interpreters need some rest as well, and second that perhaps the tapes might have to be changed, because we are already for one hour and a half in session. Yes, we have five minutes on the tape, if you can do it within five minutes that is fine. And then if the interpreters agree, and then we can have the break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has to stay anyhow over the break because of the marking of the map. So, therefore, perhaps we have a break now until 5 minutes past 1.00. Then we will have the result of the marking, and you can put your last questions. Yes. We adjourn until five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Lazic, did you manage to mark the road? We will have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if this was done under the control of both parties, may I be just permitted to point out that the northern route, the one to the north, is an alternative route mentioned by the witness as well, while the lower part was far too close to the combat lines. So it was the alternative route, the northern route, which goes outside of the map, to go around to get to Pale. That is what the witness indicated, that is what the witness said to both parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since no one objects, this certainly has been your explanation. So you had a northern more safe route, and a route closer to the confrontation lines you often would not use. Is that how I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for marking this map. It gives us an idea on how -- what route you had to take to go from Blazuj to Pale. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you had --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. These questions, I will ask them in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Witness, to a question asked by Judge El Mahdi, you answered that General Galic was speaking to -- was instructing the doctors, or rather talking about the doctors who were treating everyone regardless as a model of humanity. This is page 65 line 12 and so on in the LiveNote. Now my questions stemming from this is the following: What were the circumstances that General Galic spoke of this? Was this on a private occasion or was it something that was done more publicly? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic came to visit the hospital as a General, to visit the wounded, and he gave such statements during the visit which could be considered as an official visit an official announcement. On those occasions, what happened is that 50 per cent of the patients in hospital injured were of different -- of another ethnicity, a Croat, a Muslim, and he gave us an example of how doctors should act. So he could stress the ethical side of our profession and how wounded are treated on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, but my question was the following: It is clear in the way in which he spoke about this, but was this to one or two people that he told this or was there a larger audience? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, it wasn't a press conference hall. He spoke to the nurses, doctors, patients in the intensive care unit, in the staff room. He spoke to a gathering of doctors and patients who were in different wards. For instance, in the intensive care unit there would be sometimes 15 patients at a time, and he would say, How are you? How are you doing? And that is how it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am going to go on to the second question that I wanted to ask you, and it is the following: You said, and this is page 66, line 10 and so on, you said that the people who were injured, they could not be taken out during the day in the ambulance in 150 ambulance, if my recollection is correct. Why they could not be taken to Pale in daytime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this was -- this happened -- this was occurring before I arrived until the 1st of November, and later on it also happened that people were taken either at dusk or at night because the improvised road which was made going through the Serb municipalities all the way to Pale, went very near the demarcation line. In some places, 200, 300 metres only. I will give you an example of buildings, for instance, building in a part of town under the control of Muslim troops. This was a building that was either Batonija -- or Batonija building which was being constructed of the clinical centre. It was in the process of being in construction. From that building the, road was constantly being targeted which was about 300 metres away. So our engineers, our technicians made screens from wood, paper cardboard, to protect the vehicles from view. When vehicles were going at a distance of 800 or 1.000 metres. So the main reason was the vicinity of the other side and the lorry was quite high, and its body was quite thin, so it could be pierced through by bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In any case, was it possible to recognise these vehicles as ambulances? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ye. On the side, this vehicle had a large red cross, and I can say that this symbol didn't mean a thing during the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Dr. Lazic, this concludes your examination in this Chamber. I would like to thank you for having come a very long way to The Hague, and to answer all the questions, both of the Defence and of the Prosecution and of the Judges as well. I take it that you will find time to have this cup of coffee I deprived you of at a later stage. Thank you for coming. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Dr. Lazic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I have to say that everyone was extremely kind to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before calling your next witness, Ms. Pilipovic, we first deal with the documents that are -- two -- one -- no, the videotape you said you would not tender into evidence. You tendered that? You tendered that into evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, we do want to tender it as evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the videotape with a Roman 3 on it and something perhaps which is cassette but done in a language which is not a language I understand, and also with the figures "5" and "11" on it. That is the videotape you provided to us, yes. Perhaps it is good if you provide the videotape again, that it is always clear what exactly it is. Madam Registrar, that would have number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape is D1758/3. That is D1758/3. The English transcript of the video is D1758/3A. The map marked by witness is P3724.ML.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just have a look at the map. The original says 3274, but that is wrong. That is the wrong number, so that has been clarified that a mistake has been made on this one. So it gets a new number on it, a new sticker on it. And I have some doubts, since it has been -- it now bear as "P" number, where it is -- yes, it is presented by the Prosecution. So that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, then, before you call your next witness, I would first like to -- if there is no objections so then the video and the map marked by the witness are admitted into evidence. And I would like now to turn into closed session just for a short while before calling your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in private session which in this courtroom is the same thing as closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of October, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
